q: Where is Figure A, a chapel designed by Le Corbusier, located?
n: Figure A is Notre-Dame du Haut, Le Corbusier's chapel in Ronchamp, France (1955). Source: UNESCO (The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier).

q: Where is Figure B, an architecture school designed by Walter Gropius, located?
n: Figure B is the Bauhaus building by Walter Gropius in Dessau, Germany (1926). Source: UNESCO (Bauhaus and its Sites).

q: Where is Figure C, a residential house designed by Frank Lloyd Wright located in the USA?
n: Figure C is Fallingwater, Frank Lloyd Wright's house at Mill Run, Pennsylvania. Source: UNESCO (20th-century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright); Western Pennsylvania Conservancy.

q: Where is Figure D, completed in 1956 and designed by Mies van der Rohe, located?
n: Figure D is S.R. Crown Hall (1956) by Mies van der Rohe at IIT in Chicago, USA. Source: Illinois Institute of Technology; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Where is Figure E, designed by Oscar Niemeyer, located?
n: Figure E is Oscar Niemeyer's National Congress in Brasília, Brazil. The twin towers and the bowl and dome of the Congress are the centrepiece of Lúcio Costa's Pilot Plan for Brasília. Source: UNESCO (Brasília).

q: Who said, "Architecture should speak of its time and place, but yearn for timelessness"?
n: "Architecture should speak of its time and place, but yearn for timelessness" is a well-known quote by Frank Gehry. Source: Frank Gehry interviews (widely cited).

q: Who coined the term "biorealism"?
n: Richard Neutra coined "biorealism," linking architecture to human biology and the natural environment. Source: Neutra, Survival Through Design (1954).

q: Whose work is called "skin and bones," and who said "less is more"?
n: Mies van der Rohe's steel-frame and glass architecture is called "skin and bones," and "less is more" is his dictum. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe.

q: Who called architecture "the masterly, correct and magnificent play of masses brought together in light"?
n: Le Corbusier wrote that architecture is "the masterly, correct and magnificent play of masses brought together in light". Source: Le Corbusier, Towards a New Architecture (1923).

q: Who designed the Sagrada Família in Barcelona?
n: Antoni Gaudí took over the Sagrada Família in Barcelona in 1883 and devoted the rest of his life to it. Source: UNESCO (Works of Antoni Gaudí); Sagrada Família official site.

q: Who is known as the Father of American Architecture?
n: Benjamin Henry Latrobe, architect of the US Capitol and the Baltimore Basilica, is called the father of American architecture. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Benjamin Henry Latrobe.

q: Who is known as the Father of Modernism?
n: Louis Sullivan is called the father of modernism (and of the skyscraper), from his Chicago School work and "form follows function". Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Louis Sullivan.

q: Who designed the Guangzhou Opera House?
n: The Guangzhou Opera House (2010) was designed by Zaha Hadid. Source: Zaha Hadid Architects project page.

q: Who designed the Centre Pompidou (with Renzo Piano)?
n: The Centre Pompidou in Paris (1977) was designed by Richard Rogers with Renzo Piano. Source: Centre Pompidou official site; Pritzker Prize.

q: Which of the following is a famous dictum by Zaha Hadid?
o: Buildings are deeply emotive structures which form our psyche.
As designers, we have such power to make design change the world. We really need to make better use of our platform and do stuff that is useful.
Architecture is like writing. You have to edit it over and over so it looks effortless.
n: The quote "Architecture is like writing. You have to edit it over and over so it looks effortless" is attributed to Zaha Hadid. Source: Zaha Hadid interviews (widely cited).

q: What was Zaha Hadid's first major built project?
n: Zaha Hadid's first major built project was the Vitra Fire Station in Weil am Rhein, Germany (1993). Source: Zaha Hadid Architects; Vitra Campus.

q: Which architect won the Pritzker Prize in 2004 and the Stirling Prize in 2010 and 2011?
n: Zaha Hadid won the Pritzker Prize in 2004 and the RIBA Stirling Prize in 2010 (MAXXI) and 2011 (Evelyn Grace Academy). Source: Pritzker Architecture Prize; RIBA.

q: Which Zaha Hadid museum is in Cincinnati, Ohio?
n: Zaha Hadid's Rosenthal Center for Contemporary Art in Cincinnati, Ohio opened in 2003, her first US building. Source: Contemporary Arts Center Cincinnati; Zaha Hadid Architects.

q: Zaha Hadid's style is usually described as:
n: Zaha Hadid's style is usually described as deconstructivist, later developing into parametricism. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Zaha Hadid; MoMA Deconstructivist Architecture (1988).

q: Which Zaha Hadid project in Azerbaijan is known for its flowing curves?
n: The Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku, Azerbaijan (2012) is known for its flowing, continuous curves. Source: Zaha Hadid Architects project page.

q: Which theory did Richard Neutra develop?
n: Richard Neutra developed biorealism, design attuned to human biology and wellbeing. Source: Neutra, Survival Through Design (1954).

q: Whose work is known for trencadís, mosaic of broken tile?
n: Trencadís, a mosaic of broken tiles and ceramics, is a hallmark of Antoni Gaudí's work, as at Park Güell. Source: UNESCO (Works of Antoni Gaudí).

q: Which architect used the catenary curve throughout his work?
n: Gaudí used catenary curves and arches throughout his work, finding forms with hanging chain models. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Antoni Gaudí.

q: Who designed the Bauhaus building in Dessau?
n: Walter Gropius designed the Bauhaus building in Dessau (1926). Source: UNESCO (Bauhaus and its Sites).

q: Which architect was also an urban planner, painter, sculptor, writer and furniture designer?
n: Le Corbusier was an architect, urban planner, painter, sculptor, writer and furniture designer. Source: Fondation Le Corbusier.

q: Whose buildings are typically called "skin and bones" architecture?
n: Mies van der Rohe's buildings are called "skin and bones" architecture: an exposed steel frame with a glass skin. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe.

q: Mies van der Rohe's masterpiece, which marked the dawn of the International Style, was the Farnsworth House made of bold steel and glass. What was Mies van der Rohe’s primary role in the project?
n: Mies acted as both architect and effective contractor of the Farnsworth House, directing its construction and costs himself, which led to his dispute with the client. Source: Farnsworth House (National Trust) history.

q: Why was the Farnsworth House painted white?
o: To integrate it with nature as the only visible color
To keep out the sun's heat
n: The steel frame was painted white so the minimal glass house reads as a pure, abstract form, the only visible color against the surrounding landscape. Source: Farnsworth House (National Trust) history.

q: Which of these is a residential work of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe?
n: The Farnsworth House is one of Mies's few built houses. The Glass House is Philip Johnson's, the Villa Savoye is Le Corbusier's and the Seagram Building is an office tower. Source: Farnsworth House official site.

q: Ranked with Le Corbusier, Aalto and Wright as a master of modernism, he designed the Farnsworth House and Seagram Building. Who is he?
n: Mies van der Rohe, a master of modernism with Le Corbusier, Aalto and Wright, designed the Farnsworth House and the Seagram Building. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe.

q: Which work of Antoni Gaudí led to his cause for beatification?
n: Gaudí's lifelong devotion to the Sagrada Família led to his cause for beatification. He was declared Venerable in 2025. Source: Sagrada Família official site; Vatican Dicastery for the Causes of Saints.

q: Gaudí's Casa Milà is also known as:
n: Gaudí's Casa Milà is also known as La Pedrera ("the stone quarry"). Source: UNESCO (Works of Antoni Gaudí).

q: Gaudi's intent in designing this structure was to create a:
n: Gaudí intended the Sagrada Família as a spiritual symbol, a "Bible in stone" expressing faith. Source: Sagrada Família official site.

q: Heis known as the Father of Fantastic Architecture.
n: Antoni Gaudí is often called the father of fantastic architecture for his imaginative, organic forms. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Antoni Gaudí.

q: Which Art Nouveau (Modernisme) architect designed the Palau Güell in Barcelona?
n: Antoni Gaudí designed the Palau Güell in Barcelona (1886–88), a Modernisme work. Source: UNESCO (Works of Antoni Gaudí).

q: Which Gaudí work is nicknamed "The Quarry"?
n: Casa Milà is nicknamed "La Pedrera" (The Quarry). The name refers to its rough, undulating limestone facade, which looks like an open quarry face. Source: UNESCO (Works of Antoni Gaudí).
